clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in GNAO1, which encodes the alpha subunit of the inhibitory heterotrimeric G-protein Galpha-o, abundant in the developing brain and central to neurotransmitter signalling
Presents along a spectrum from an early infantile epileptic encephalopathy to a predominant movement disorder without prominent seizures
The movement disorder is a hallmark: chorea, dystonia, and choreoathetosis that can escalate into life-threatening dystonic or choreic storms requiring intensive care
Seizures, when present, begin in infancy and can be focal, tonic, or epileptic spasms, often with a poorly organised or suppression-burst electroencephalogram
Development is typically impaired with hypotonia, poor head control, and later feeding and communication difficulties

Movement exacerbations may be provoked by illness, stress, or changes in medication and can require sedation, dopamine-pathway agents, or deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus in refractory cases
Genotype influences phenotype, with certain variants biased towards epilepsy-predominant and others towards movement-disorder-predominant disease
reference.pathophysiology: GNAO1 encodes Galpha-o, the most abundant G-protein alpha subunit in the mammalian brain, which couples to numerous G-protein-coupled receptors and modulates neurotransmitter release and downstream signalling, including adenylate cyclase and calcium and potassium channel regulation. Disease variants disturb this signalling through loss- or gain-of-function-like effects on the G-protein cycle, perturbing the balance of inhibitory and excitatory transmission in basal ganglia and cortical circuits. This disruption produces both the epileptic and the striking hyperkinetic movement features, and the particular variant helps determine whether epilepsy or movement disorder dominates.
additionalDifferentials: PDE10A and other genetic chorea syndromes
Mitochondrial and metabolic encephalopathies with dystonia
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to confirm the GNAO1 variant
Video electroencephalography where seizures are suspected
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural and metabolic causes
Movement disorder characterisation, including video documentation of chorea and dystonia
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics
Assessment for deep brain stimulation candidacy in refractory movement disorder
redFlags: Dystonic or choreic storm with hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, or cardiorespiratory compromise
Status epilepticus in the epilepsy-predominant phenotype
Rapid feeding deterioration with aspiration risk
Escalating involuntary movements unresponsive to standard therapy
reference.prognosis: Most affected children have significant intellectual disability and persistent movement disorder; life-threatening dyskinetic crises contribute to morbidity, and while deep brain stimulation can markedly reduce refractory movements, cognitive impairment usually persists.
pitfalls: Mistaking the dyskinetic phenotype for dyskinetic cerebral palsy and missing the genetic diagnosis
Under-recognising a dystonic storm as an emergency requiring escalation and intensive support
Focusing only on seizures while neglecting the disabling movement disorder
Failing to consider deep brain stimulation in medically refractory dyskinesia
references: ILAE and movement disorder society resources on GNAO1 encephalopathy
management: Treat seizures with broad-spectrum antiseizure medication titrated to the seizure type and electroencephalographic pattern
Manage chorea and dystonia with dopamine-depleting or dopamine-blocking agents such as tetrabenazine and other movement-disorder drugs
Recognise and treat life-threatening dystonic or choreic storms as emergencies with benzodiazepines, sedation and intensive care support
Consider deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus internus for refractory, disabling movement disorder
Provide developmental and rehabilitative support with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy and feeding support or gastrostomy
Identify and avoid exacerbating triggers such as intercurrent illness, stress and abrupt medication change, and offer genetic counselling given usually de novo variants
